cards.title: BigQuery — Serverless Data Warehouse
cards.teaser: BigQuery is Google Cloud's fully serverless, petabyte-scale analytical database. You write SQL; Google manages the infrastructure. There are no clusters to provision, no indexes to tune, and no knobs to turn — just queries against data at any scale.

runs.text: BigQuery

was introduced in 2010 and open-sourced as Apache Dremel. Its key architectural insight is the separation of storage from compute: data lives in Google's Colossus distributed filesystem; compute (query execution) is allocated on-demand and released immediately after a query completes.
What BigQuery does in a single sentence: you point SQL at terabytes of data in Cloud Storage or native tables and get results in seconds. Core properties:

items.text: Serverless
— no cluster management, no JDBC connection pools, no capacity planning for normal workloads.
Petabyte-scale
— Google processes exabytes internally with Dremel. Public BigQuery regularly handles tables in the hundreds of terabytes.
Standard SQL
— fully ANSI-compliant SQL with window functions, ARRAY/STRUCT types, JSON functions, and GIS extensions.
Integrated ecosystem
— native connectors for Dataflow, Dataproc, Vertex AI, Looker, and external tables over Cloud Storage, Bigtable, and Google Sheets.

runs.text: A minimal query against a public dataset:

explanation.text:
SELECT
  departure_airport,
  COUNT(*) AS flight_count,
  AVG(arrival_delay) AS avg_delay_min
FROM `bigquery-samples.airline_ontime_data.flights`
WHERE year = 2023
GROUP BY departure_airport
ORDER BY avg_delay_min DESC
LIMIT 20;

runs.text: This query scans the subset of columns referenced (not the full table row) because BigQuery uses columnar storage — covered in the next card.
BigQuery bills on bytes scanned (on-demand) or reserved slots (flat-rate). Always use SELECT on specific columns rather than SELECT * to minimize cost.

BigQuery is a SQL engine that runs on Google's infrastructure. You give it a query, it spins up thousands of workers across your data, returns results, and shuts everything down — you never see any of that machinery.

cards.title: BigQuery Storage — Capacitor Format
cards.teaser: BigQuery stores data in Capacitor, a proprietary columnar format optimized for analytical reads. Columns are stored separately, compressed independently, and encoded with run-length and dictionary schemes — making full-table row scans essentially obsolete.

runs.text: Understanding BigQuery's storage layer explains most of its performance and cost characteristics. Native BigQuery tables use the
Capacitor
format, which is a proprietary columnar format built on top of Google's Colossus filesystem.

items.text: Columnar layout
— all values for a single column are stored together. A query asking for two columns out of 100 reads roughly 2% of the stored data.
Compression per column

— each column is compressed independently using encodings tuned to its data type (run-length encoding for low-cardinality string columns, dictionary encoding for repeated values, delta encoding for timestamps).
Nested and repeated fields
— Capacitor natively encodes STRUCT and ARRAY columns using Dremel's record-shredding algorithm, so deeply nested JSON-like data doesn't require a separate denormalization step.
Automatic micro-partitioning

— BigQuery clusters data physically via table partitioning (by date, range, or ingestion time) and clustering (by up to four columns). These are not indexes — they reduce bytes scanned by skipping irrelevant file segments.

runs.text: Storage pricing has two tiers:

items.text: Active storage
(~$0.02/GB/month) — tables or partitions modified in the last 90 days.
Long-term storage
(~$0.01/GB/month) — tables or partitions not modified for 90+ days; automatically halved price.

runs.text: Best practices for storage efficiency:

explanation.text:
-- Partitioned + clustered table definition
CREATE TABLE `myproject.mydataset.events`
(
  event_id STRING,
  user_id  STRING,
  event_ts TIMESTAMP,
  payload  JSON
)
PARTITION BY DATE(event_ts)
CLUSTER BY user_id
OPTIONS (partition_expiration_days = 365);

runs.text: Always partition large tables. A WHERE clause on the partition column lets BigQuery skip entire file segments before scanning begins — this is called partition pruning and can reduce query cost by orders of magnitude.

BigQuery stores each column of your table separately in Capacitor. When your query asks for three columns, it reads only those three columns' worth of bytes — not the full rows. That's why analytical queries are fast and cheap: you don't pay for data you don't touch.

cards.title: BigQuery Compute — Slots, On-Demand vs Reservations
cards.teaser: BigQuery compute is measured in slots — virtual CPUs that execute query stages in parallel. On-demand pricing charges per byte scanned; reservations (flat-rate) buy a fixed number of slots and are right for predictable, high-volume workloads.

runs.text: A
slot

is BigQuery's unit of compute: one slot is roughly one vCPU with associated memory. BigQuery automatically decomposes a query into a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of stages and executes stages in parallel across as many slots as needed and available.

items.text: On-demand pricing
— $5–$7 per TB of data scanned. BigQuery auto-scales slots up to a project-level quota (typically 2,000 slots). Good for ad-hoc exploration and variable workloads.
Editions (reservations)

— introduced in 2023, replacing legacy flat-rate. Buy a baseline of slots per hour at a committed price. Three tiers: Standard, Enterprise, Enterprise Plus (adds BI Engine acceleration and cross-region disaster recovery).
Autoscaler
— reservations can auto-scale above baseline up to a configured maximum, combining predictability with elasticity.
Slot commitments
— 1-year or 3-year commitments reduce hourly slot cost by ~25–45% vs pay-as-you-go editions.

runs.text: Choosing between on-demand and reservations:

items.text: On-demand
— best when queries are infrequent, data scanned is small, or workloads are unpredictable. Zero upfront commitment.
Reservations
— best when you run continuous pipelines, have SLA-bound dashboards, or process >100 TB/day. Also enables cross-project slot sharing within an organization.

runs.text: On-demand queries that scan the entire table (SELECT *) can produce surprising invoices on multi-TB tables. Use INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS to audit bytes billed before queries hit production.
Think of slots as workers. On-demand lets you borrow as many workers as needed and pay per job. Reservations mean you hire a fixed team full-time — more predictable cost, better for steady workloads.

cards.title: BigQuery ML — SQL-Driven Machine Learning
cards.teaser: BigQuery ML lets you train, evaluate, and run inference on ML models using standard SQL — no Python, no notebooks, no data export. The model lives in BigQuery, trained on BigQuery data, and predictions run as SQL queries.

runs.text: BigQuery ML (BQML) brings ML training inside the data warehouse. The key value proposition: analysts who know SQL can build models without moving data to a separate ML platform.

Supported model types include linear regression, logistic regression, K-means clustering, time-series forecasting (ARIMA+), matrix factorization, deep neural networks (via TensorFlow), boosted trees (XGBoost), and imported TensorFlow/scikit-learn models.
Full BQML workflow in SQL:

explanation.text:
-- 1. Train a logistic regression model
CREATE OR REPLACE MODEL `myproject.mydataset.churn_model`
OPTIONS(
  model_type = 'LOGISTIC_REG',
  input_label_cols = ['churned'],
  max_iterations = 20,
  auto_class_weights = TRUE
) AS
SELECT
  days_since_last_login,
  total_purchases,
  avg_order_value,
  support_tickets_opened,
  churned
FROM `myproject.mydataset.user_features`
WHERE split = 'TRAIN';

-- 2. Evaluate the model
SELECT *
FROM ML.EVALUATE(
  MODEL `myproject.mydataset.churn_model`,
  (SELECT * FROM `myproject.mydataset.user_features` WHERE split = 'TEST')
);

-- 3. Batch inference
SELECT
  user_id,
  predicted_churned,
  predicted_churned_probs
FROM ML.PREDICT(
  MODEL `myproject.mydataset.churn_model`,
  (SELECT * FROM `myproject.mydataset.active_users`)
);

runs.text: BQML also supports
remote models
— you can call Vertex AI endpoints or Cloud AI APIs (Vision, Natural Language, Translation) directly from SQL via
ML.PREDICT
on a
REMOTE MODEL
, keeping all orchestration inside BigQuery.
BQML is best for structured, tabular data at warehouse scale. For unstructured data, computer vision, or custom neural architectures requiring GPU training, use Vertex AI Training instead.

BigQuery ML lets you say CREATE MODEL in SQL, train on your BigQuery data, and run predictions as a SELECT. No Python environment, no data pipeline to a separate ML system — it all stays inside the warehouse.

cards.title: BigQuery Omni — Cross-Cloud Query
cards.teaser: BigQuery Omni runs BigQuery's query engine directly on AWS (S3) and Azure (ADLS Gen2) data without copying it to GCP. You write the same SQL you'd use on GCP; BigQuery executes workers in the foreign cloud.

runs.text: BigQuery Omni solves a specific pain: organizations with data in AWS S3 or Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 who want to run SQL analytics without paying egress fees to move petabytes to GCP.
Architecture:

items.text: BigQuery control plane stays on GCP
— query parsing, job management, IAM authorization all happen in GCP.
Compute workers deploy into the remote cloud
— Omni runs managed BigQuery workers in AWS or Azure regions via Anthos (now GKE-based). Data never leaves the foreign cloud during scan.
Results returned to GCP
— only query results (typically small) cross cloud boundaries. Scanning happens locally to the data.

runs.text: Usage example — querying S3-backed external tables:

explanation.text:
-- Create an AWS connection (set up once via Cloud Console)
-- Then define an external table pointing to S3
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE `myproject.aws_dataset.sales_data`
WITH CONNECTION `aws-us-east-1.myproject.aws-conn`
OPTIONS (
  format = 'PARQUET',
  uris = ['s3://my-bucket/sales/year=2024/*']
);

-- Query cross-cloud just like any BigQuery table
SELECT region, SUM(revenue) AS total_revenue
FROM `myproject.aws_dataset.sales_data`
GROUP BY region;

items.text: Supported formats
— Parquet, ORC, Avro, CSV, JSON on S3 and ADLS Gen2.
Limitations
— Omni tables are read-only external tables; you cannot INSERT or UPDATE foreign-cloud data via BigQuery. Cross-cloud JOIN performance depends on network latency between clouds.

runs.text: BigQuery Omni is a good fit for multi-cloud analytics and data mesh scenarios where different business units own data in different clouds and a single governance layer (BigQuery IAM) is desirable.

BigQuery Omni is like a remote server that runs BigQuery workers inside AWS or Azure, next to your S3 or ADLS data. You write normal SQL on GCP; the scan happens in the other cloud; only the answer comes back.

cards.title: Dataflow — Apache Beam Fully Managed
cards.teaser: Dataflow is Google Cloud's fully managed execution engine for Apache Beam pipelines. One Beam pipeline definition runs in batch mode over historical data or streaming mode over live data — Dataflow manages autoscaling, workers, and fault tolerance.

runs.text: Apache Beam (Batch + strEAM) is an open-source unified programming model for data pipelines. You write a Beam pipeline once in Python, Java, or Go; you then choose a runner — Dataflow on GCP, Flink, Spark, or the local direct runner for testing.
Dataflow's managed value:

items.text: No cluster management
— Dataflow provisions, scales, and decommissions workers automatically. Workers auto-scale mid-job based on throughput.
Unified batch + streaming
— the same pipeline code handles both modes. Beam's watermark model handles late-arriving events in streaming.
Exactly-once semantics
— Dataflow streaming pipelines guarantee exactly-once delivery to BigQuery and Pub/Sub sinks.
Dataflow Prime
— vertical autoscaling (adjusts worker memory mid-job), right-fitting (matches machine type to pipeline profile), and Hot Key Fanout (splits skewed keys to avoid stragglers).

runs.text: Pseudocode for a streaming Pub/Sub-to-BigQuery pipeline:

explanation.text:
import apache_beam as beam
from apache_beam.options.pipeline_options import PipelineOptions

options = PipelineOptions(
    runner='DataflowRunner',
    project='myproject',
    region='us-central1',
    streaming=True
)

with beam.Pipeline(options=options) as p:
    (
        p
        | 'ReadFromPubSub' >> beam.io.ReadFromPubSub(
            subscription='projects/myproject/subscriptions/events-sub'
          )
        | 'ParseJSON'  >> beam.Map(lambda msg: json.loads(msg.decode()))
        | 'FilterValid' >> beam.Filter(lambda e: e.get('user_id') is not None)
        | 'EnrichEvent' >> beam.Map(enrich_with_user_profile)
        | 'WindowInto'  >> beam.WindowInto(beam.window.FixedWindows(60))
        | 'WriteToBQ'   >> beam.io.WriteToBigQuery(
            'myproject:analytics.events',
            write_disposition=beam.io.BigQueryDisposition.WRITE_APPEND
          )
    )

runs.text: Dataflow Flex Templates package your pipeline as a Docker image, enabling parameterized job submission without building from source at launch time. Use Flex Templates for production pipelines triggered by Cloud Scheduler or Workflows.

You write a Beam pipeline that says 'read from here, transform this way, write there.' Dataflow takes that definition, fires up hundreds of workers in GCP, runs the job — batch or streaming — and shuts everything down when done. You never touch a cluster.

cards.title: Pub/Sub — Global Asynchronous Messaging
cards.teaser: Cloud Pub/Sub is a fully managed, globally distributed message bus. Publishers push messages to a topic; subscribers pull from subscriptions. It decouples producers from consumers, handles any throughput, and durably stores messages for up to 7 days.

runs.text: Pub/Sub is Google's answer to Apache Kafka for most cloud-native use cases. It handles the ingestion layer of real-time analytics architectures: events arrive at Pub/Sub, then flow to Dataflow or Dataproc for processing.
Core concepts:

items.text: Topic
— named feed to which publishers send messages. A topic has no defined consumer; many subscriptions can attach to one topic.
Subscription
— durable cursor into a topic. A subscription can be
push
(Pub/Sub delivers to an HTTP endpoint) or
pull
(consumer polls). Unacknowledged messages are redelivered.
At-least-once delivery
— Pub/Sub guarantees delivery but may duplicate. Applications must be idempotent or use message IDs for deduplication.
Global replication
— topics replicate across multiple GCP regions automatically. No partition assignment or replication factor to configure.
Ordering keys
— messages with the same ordering key are delivered in publish order to a subscription, enabling use cases like CDC (change data capture).

runs.text: Pub/Sub in the analytics pipeline:

explanation.text:
Sources → Pub/Sub topic → [Subscription A] → Dataflow → BigQuery
                       → [Subscription B] → Cloud Functions (alerting)
                       → [Subscription C] → Cloud Storage (raw archive)

runs.text: Multiple independent systems read the same event stream without coupling or contention, because each subscription is an independent cursor.

Pub/Sub auto-scales to millions of messages per second with no configuration. The practical comparison with Kafka: Pub/Sub removes all infrastructure (brokers, ZooKeeper, partition management) at the cost of less control over ordering and consumer group semantics.

Pub/Sub is a message post-box: anyone can drop a message in a topic, and any number of subscribers can each independently read every message. Google manages the post-box — no servers, no partitions, no replication factor.

cards.title: Pub/Sub Lite — Zone-Scoped, Cost-Optimized Messaging
cards.teaser: Pub/Sub Lite is a cheaper, zone-scoped variant of Pub/Sub. You pre-provision throughput capacity and storage, trade global replication for single-zone placement, and pay ~10x less per GB than standard Pub/Sub for predictable high-throughput workloads.

runs.text: Pub/Sub Lite is designed for teams who need Kafka-style economics — provisioned, predictable cost — without running Kafka themselves. The trade-offs are explicit:

items.text: Zone-scoped (not global)
— a Lite topic lives in a single zone. If that zone is unavailable, the topic is unavailable. No cross-region replication.
Provisioned capacity
— you set publish throughput (MiB/s) and subscribe throughput (MiB/s) at topic creation. You pay for that capacity whether used or not.
Explicit storage quota
— you provision GiB of message storage. Messages are retained until the quota is full or the retention window expires, whichever comes first.
Partition model
— like Kafka, Lite uses explicit partitions. Consumers are assigned partitions, enabling ordered, parallel consumption.

runs.text: When to use Pub/Sub vs Pub/Sub Lite:

items.text: Use standard Pub/Sub
— when global reliability is required, throughput is unpredictable or bursty, or operational simplicity is the priority.
Use Pub/Sub Lite
— when throughput is steady and high (>100 MB/s), you need long message retention (days to weeks), per-message ordering within a partition is required, and cost per GB is the primary constraint.

runs.text: Pub/Sub Lite does not support push subscriptions — only pull. You must run a consumer process. Applications that rely on Pub/Sub's push-to-HTTP-endpoint pattern cannot use Lite.

Pub/Sub Lite is Pub/Sub's cheaper sibling: you give up global redundancy and get a Kafka-like provisioned capacity model in a single zone. Right choice when you have constant high-volume traffic and a tight budget.

cards.title: Dataproc — Managed Spark, Hadoop, and Flink
cards.teaser: Dataproc is Google Cloud's managed service for running Apache Spark, Hadoop, Flink, and Presto clusters. You provision a cluster in ~90 seconds, run jobs, and delete it — paying only for the time the cluster exists.

runs.text: Dataproc targets teams with existing Spark or Hadoop workloads who want to run them on GCP without re-architecting. It is
not
a fully managed, serverless service like BigQuery — you still choose machine types, worker counts, and cluster configurations. But compared to self-managed Hadoop/Spark:

items.text: Fast cluster creation
— ~90 seconds vs hours for on-premises cluster commissioning.
Ephemeral clusters
— clusters are disposable. Spin up for a job, delete after. No idle cluster cost. Data lives in Cloud Storage (GCS), not HDFS.
Preemptible and Spot VMs
— secondary workers can use Spot VMs (80% discount) for fault-tolerant batch jobs, reducing cluster cost significantly.
Versioned images
— Dataproc images bundle Spark, Hadoop, Hive, and Pig at specific versions. Custom images extend the base image for pre-installed dependencies.

runs.text: Dataproc Serverless (Spark) removes cluster management entirely — submit a Spark batch job without provisioning a cluster. Google manages worker allocation, scaling, and teardown. Suitable for Spark SQL and PySpark batch jobs that don't require interactive sessions.
BigQuery vs Dataproc decision:

items.text: Choose BigQuery
— for SQL analytics, BQML, standard ETL. Fully serverless, no cluster config.
Choose Dataproc
— for migrating existing Spark/Hadoop jobs, complex custom transformations in PySpark, Hive metastore compatibility, or Flink streaming jobs.

runs.text: Store Dataproc job data in Cloud Storage, not HDFS. GCS is durable, cheaper, and accessible after the cluster is deleted. HDFS on Dataproc is an ephemeral local disk — data is lost when the cluster is deleted.

Dataproc gives you a managed Spark or Hadoop cluster on GCP. You still pick the cluster size, but Google handles OS, Spark version, and cluster health. Spin it up, run the job, delete it — pay only for the hours it ran.

cards.title: Composer — Managed Apache Airflow
cards.teaser: Cloud Composer is a fully managed orchestration service built on Apache Airflow. You write DAGs in Python; Composer runs the scheduler, workers, metadata database, and web UI — eliminating the operational burden of self-managed Airflow.

runs.text: Apache Airflow is the de facto standard for workflow orchestration: you define a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) of tasks in Python, set dependencies, and Airflow executes them in order. Cloud Composer is the managed flavor.
What Composer manages:

items.text: Airflow scheduler and executor
— runs on GKE. Composer 2 uses auto-scaling for workers, so idle environments cost less.
Metadata database
— backed by Cloud SQL (PostgreSQL). Stores DAG run history, task states, and logs.
Web server (Airflow UI)
— accessible via IAP-protected HTTPS. Provides DAG monitoring, task logs, and trigger controls.
DAG storage
— DAG Python files live in a Cloud Storage bucket. Uploading a file automatically syncs to the environment.

runs.text: Common Composer pattern — GCS event triggers BigQuery load:

explanation.text:
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.operators.bigquery import BigQueryInsertJobOperator
from airflow.providers.google.cloud.sensors.gcs import GCSObjectExistenceSensor
from datetime import datetime

with DAG('daily_sales_load', schedule='@daily', start_date=datetime(2024, 1, 1)) as dag:

    wait_for_file = GCSObjectExistenceSensor(
        task_id='wait_for_sales_file',
        bucket='my-data-bucket',
        object='sales/{{ ds }}/sales_data.parquet',
        timeout=3600
    )

    load_to_bq = BigQueryInsertJobOperator(
        task_id='load_sales_to_bq',
        configuration={
            'load': {
                'sourceUris': ['gs://my-data-bucket/sales/{{ ds }}/sales_data.parquet'],
                'destinationTable': {'projectId': 'myproject', 'datasetId': 'sales', 'tableId': 'daily_sales'},
                'sourceFormat': 'PARQUET',
                'writeDisposition': 'WRITE_APPEND'
            }
        }
    )

    wait_for_file >> load_to_bq

runs.text: Composer 2 is significantly cheaper than Composer 1 for environments that are mostly idle. Composer 2 auto-scales workers to zero between runs. Choose Composer 2 for all new environments.

Composer is Airflow-as-a-service. You write Python DAGs that describe your data pipeline tasks and their order; Composer runs the scheduler, the workers, and the UI. You don't manage Airflow's database or infrastructure.

cards.title: Looker and Looker Studio — BI and Dashboards
cards.teaser: Looker is Google Cloud's enterprise BI platform using LookML to define semantic data models. Looker Studio (formerly Data Studio) is the free, lightweight dashboarding tool. They serve different segments of the analytics stack.

runs.text: Google Cloud offers two BI products that are commonly confused:

items.text: Looker

— acquired by Google in 2020. Enterprise-grade BI platform. Uses LookML, a YAML-based semantic modeling language, to define metrics, dimensions, joins, and business logic centrally. All data stays in BigQuery (or other databases) — Looker queries live; it does not copy or cache data. Provides embedded analytics APIs, scheduled delivers, alerts, and a governed metric layer.
Looker Studio

— free, self-service dashboarding tool (no-code). Connects to BigQuery, Google Analytics, Google Sheets, and 800+ community connectors. Suitable for quick departmental dashboards, individual reporting, and embedding in web pages. No LookML, no semantic layer.

runs.text: LookML example defining a metric:
Decision guide:

items.text: Looker
— large organizations needing a single source of truth for metrics, embedded analytics in products, or governed access to sensitive data.
Looker Studio
— individuals and small teams who need fast, free dashboards without IT involvement.

runs.text: Looker is enterprise BI where analysts define metrics in code (LookML) so the whole company agrees on what 'revenue' means. Looker Studio is a free drag-and-drop dashboard builder. Same Google family, very different tools.

cards.title: Analytics Hub — Data Marketplace and Sharing
cards.teaser: Analytics Hub is BigQuery's managed data marketplace. Publishers list datasets as data exchanges; subscribers subscribe and get a linked dataset that appears in their BigQuery project — data is never copied, IAM governs access, and the publisher retains control.

runs.text: Analytics Hub addresses a fundamental enterprise data problem: organizations produce valuable datasets that multiple teams or external partners need, but sharing via export, email, or copy creates governance nightmares. Analytics Hub solves this with a publish-subscribe model on top of BigQuery.
Key concepts:

items.text: Exchange
— a curated catalog of datasets. An exchange can be private (internal org), restricted (specific organizations), or public (Google-hosted public data).
Listing
— a discoverable entry in an exchange pointing to a BigQuery dataset. Listings include descriptions, metadata, sample queries, and access request workflows.
Linked dataset
— when a subscriber subscribes to a listing, they receive a linked dataset in their own project. It is a live, read-only reference to the publisher's dataset — no data copy, always current.
Publisher control
— publisher revokes access by removing the subscriber from the listing. The linked dataset immediately becomes inaccessible.

runs.text: Use cases:

items.text: Internal data mesh
— data product teams publish canonical datasets (customer 360, product catalog) that other teams subscribe to without requesting data exports.
External data monetization
— companies publish enriched datasets to paying customers via a private exchange.
Google public datasets
— Google uses Analytics Hub to publish free public datasets (weather, financial, genomics) queryable directly in BigQuery.

runs.text: Analytics Hub integrates with Dataplex for automated data discovery and governance tagging on shared datasets. Listings can inherit Dataplex data quality scores and lineage metadata.

Analytics Hub is an App Store for BigQuery datasets. Publishers list their data; subscribers click subscribe and get a live read-only view in their own project. No copying, no ETL — the publisher always controls who can see what.

cards.title: Dataplex — Data Fabric, Governance, and Lineage
cards.teaser: Dataplex is Google Cloud's intelligent data fabric. It organizes data across BigQuery, Cloud Storage, and other sources into logical lakes and zones, enforces metadata standards, runs automated data quality checks, and tracks data lineage end to end.

runs.text: As organizations accumulate data across dozens of projects, buckets, and datasets, governance breaks down: nobody knows where data lives, whether it's current, or who owns it. Dataplex provides the organizational and governance layer on top of existing storage.
Dataplex structure:

items.text: Lake
— top-level organizational unit. A lake typically maps to a business domain (e.g., Customer, Finance, Operations).
Zone
— subdivision within a lake. Raw zone (landing data), curated zone (validated, transformed). Zones enforce data format constraints (e.g., curated zone requires Parquet or Avro, not raw CSV).
Asset
— a Cloud Storage bucket or BigQuery dataset attached to a zone. Dataplex discovers tables and files automatically.

runs.text: Governance features:

items.text: Data quality checks
— Dataplex runs SQL-based quality rules (null checks, range checks, referential integrity) on a schedule and publishes results to BigQuery.
Data lineage
— automatically captures lineage from BigQuery, Dataflow, and Spark jobs. Surfaces a visual graph of: which tables feed which downstream tables.
Metadata tagging
— tag templates attach structured metadata (PII classification, data owner, SLA tier) to tables and columns. Tags are searchable via Data Catalog.
Unified discovery
— integrates with Data Catalog (now part of Dataplex). Search across all GCP data assets by name, tag, column name, or description.

runs.text: Dataplex lineage is particularly valuable for GDPR compliance: when a right-to-erasure request arrives, lineage shows every downstream table that derived from the affected user record.

Dataplex is the map of your data landscape. It organizes your GCS buckets and BigQuery datasets into labeled zones, checks data quality automatically, and draws the lineage graph showing where every table's data originally came from.

cards.title: BigLake — Unified Storage Across BigQuery, Cloud Storage, and Multi-Cloud
cards.teaser: BigLake extends BigQuery's security and governance model to data that lives outside BigQuery tables — Cloud Storage files, Amazon S3, and Azure ADLS Gen2. One access control layer governs structured tables and raw files alike.

runs.text: BigLake solves the governance split between lakehouse and warehouse. Before BigLake, a BigQuery table had row-level and column-level IAM; a Cloud Storage bucket had bucket-level IAM. The same data, stored differently, had wildly different security postures.
What BigLake does:

items.text: Uniform security model

— BigLake tables defined over GCS, S3, or ADLS inherit BigQuery's row-level and column-level security policies. A user can be granted access to specific columns of a Parquet file without ever having GCS read access to the bucket.
Query via BigQuery or open formats
— BigLake tables are queryable from BigQuery SQL, Spark (via BigQuery Storage API), and Vertex AI. The same table definition serves multiple compute engines.
Open format support
— supports Parquet, ORC, Avro, CSV, JSON files on GCS, and files on S3/ADLS Gen2 via BigQuery Omni connections.
Table ACL without data copy
— sharing a BigLake table grants access at the BigQuery policy layer; direct GCS/S3 access can remain locked. This is the principal advantage over plain external tables.

runs.text: End-to-end analytics architecture using all the services in this chapter:

explanation.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SOURCES                                                        │
│  App Events ──► Pub/Sub Topic ──► Pub/Sub Subscription          │
│  DB CDC     ──► Pub/Sub Lite  ──► Dataflow (Beam pipeline)      │
│  Batch Files──► Cloud Storage ──┐  │                            │
│  S3/ADLS    ──► BigLake Tables ─┤  │                            │
└────────────────────────────────┼──┼────────────────────────────┘
                                 │  │
┌────────────────────────────────▼──▼────────────────────────────┐
│  PROCESSING                                                     │
│  Dataflow ──────────────────────► BigQuery (native tables)      │
│  Dataproc (Spark/Flink) ────────► BigQuery (via BQ Storage API) │
│  Composer (Airflow DAGs) orchestrates all above jobs            │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                 │
┌────────────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────┐
│  SERVING & GOVERNANCE                                            │
│  BigQuery ML   ── in-warehouse model training + inference        │
│  BigQuery Omni ── cross-cloud SQL (AWS/Azure)                    │
│  Analytics Hub ── governed dataset sharing / data marketplace    │
│  Dataplex      ── data quality, lineage, metadata tagging        │
│  Looker        ── semantic layer + enterprise BI                 │

runs.text: BigLake is the bridge that makes the GCP analytics stack a genuine lakehouse: open format files on cheap object storage, governed and queried with the same SQL and IAM as a fully managed warehouse table.

BigLake lets you wrap a Parquet file on S3 or GCS in a BigQuery security policy. Analysts query it with SQL, Spark reads it via the BigQuery API, and the GCS bucket itself stays locked. Governance travels with the table definition, not the storage.
